title: Scientists Burned Their Own Scrolls to Read 2,000-Year-Old Ones
mediaSource: Herculaneum carbonized scroll papyrus X ray CT Berkeley lead ink

scenes.title: To read ancient burned books, scientists burned new ones
scenes.narration: Researchers recreated and carbonized modern papyrus scrolls to test a method for reading ancient scrolls buried by Mount Vesuvius.

scenes.title: The originals can crumble if opened
scenes.narration: The Herculaneum scrolls were carbonized in the eruption of 79 CE and are so fragile that physically unrolling them can destroy them.

scenes.title: The team recreated the disaster in a furnace
scenes.narration: They wrote on real papyrus with traditional-style ink, rolled it up, and carbonized it in a hot low-oxygen chamber.

scenes.title: Lead in ink lights up under X-rays
scenes.narration: Even tiny amounts of lead made the letters absorb far more X-rays than the charred papyrus, making the writing much easier to detect.
keywords: X ray tomography papyrus lead ink

scenes.title: Some ancient inks really did contain metals
scenes.narration: Researchers have already found lead or copper in some ancient papyrus inks, raising hopes that the same approach could work on Herculaneum texts.
keywords: ancient papyrus XRF lead copper ink

scenes.title: Books thought lost to fire may still be readable
scenes.narration: If the right inks are present, ancient books could be read without ever physically opening the fragile scrolls.
